learningObjectives.title: The end of the Cold War

questions.q: When was the Yalta Conference, at which the 'Big Three' met to plan the post-war world, held?
questions.explain: The Yalta Conference took place in February 1945 while the Second World War was still being fought in Europe.

questions.q: Who represented the United States for most of the Potsdam Conference in July 1945?
questions.explain: Roosevelt had died in April 1945, so the new president Harry Truman represented the USA at Potsdam.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the Truman Doctrine of 1947?
options: To contain the spread of communism by supporting free peoples resisting it
To create a single European currency
To give the USSR economic aid
questions.explain: The Truman Doctrine committed the USA to a policy of containment, pledging support to nations threatened by communism.

questions.q: Which organisation did the USSR set up in 1949 as its economic answer to Marshall Aid?
questions.explain: Comecon (the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance) was created in 1949 to coordinate the economies of the Eastern Bloc.

questions.q: What action by the Western powers most directly triggered Stalin's blockade of West Berlin in 1948?
options: The introduction of a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, in the western zones
The building of the Berlin Wall
questions.explain: Stalin blockaded Berlin partly in response to the western zones being merged and a new currency introduced without Soviet agreement.

questions.q: West Berlin was cut off by land in 1948, yet the Western powers avoided using force. Which response did they choose?
options: Flying supplies into West Berlin by air
Sending tanks along the blockaded roads
Launching an air strike on Soviet troops
questions.explain: The Berlin Airlift supplied the city by air for almost a year, avoiding direct conflict until Stalin lifted the blockade in 1949.

questions.q: In which year was NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) founded?
questions.explain: NATO was established in 1949 as a Western military alliance based on collective defence.

questions.q: Who was the reformist leader of the Hungarian government during the 1956 uprising?
questions.explain: Imre Nagy led the reforms during the 1956 Hungarian Uprising and was later executed after the Soviet crackdown.

questions.q: Which decision by Nagy most alarmed the USSR and helped provoke the Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956?
options: His announcement that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact
His signing of the Marshall Plan
His building of a wall around Budapest
questions.explain: Nagy's plan to withdraw Hungary from the Warsaw Pact and become neutral was unacceptable to the USSR, which then invaded.

questions.q: What was the main reason the East German government built the Berlin Wall in 1961?
options: To stop skilled East Germans fleeing to the West through Berlin
To defend against a NATO invasion
questions.explain: The Wall was built to halt the large flow of East Germans, especially skilled workers, escaping to the West via Berlin.

questions.q: Why did Khrushchev place nuclear missiles on Cuba in 1962?
options: To defend Cuba and offset US missiles based in Turkey and Italy
To start a nuclear war with the USA
To blockade the coast of Florida
questions.explain: The missiles were meant to protect communist Cuba and redress the imbalance created by US missiles near the USSR's borders.

questions.q: How did President Kennedy choose to respond when US spy planes discovered Soviet missiles on Cuba?
options: An instant nuclear strike on the USSR
Withdrawing all US forces from Europe
questions.explain: Kennedy imposed a naval 'quarantine' to stop further Soviet ships reaching Cuba while pursuing a diplomatic solution.

questions.q: The Cuban Missile Crisis was resolved through a compromise. Which outcome best describes the settlement?
options: The USSR removed its missiles from Cuba; the USA pledged not to invade Cuba and secretly removed missiles from Turkey
The USA invaded Cuba and removed Castro
The USSR kept its missiles in Cuba permanently
questions.explain: Khrushchev withdrew the missiles in return for a US promise not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove missiles from Turkey.

questions.q: Who led the reform movement known as the 'Prague Spring' in Czechoslovakia in 1968?
questions.explain: Alexander Dubček led the 1968 reforms aiming for 'socialism with a human face' before Warsaw Pact forces intervened.

questions.q: The Brezhnev Doctrine claimed the USSR could intervene in any Warsaw Pact state where socialism was threatened. Which action was justified using it?
options: The Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968
The launch of the Marshall Plan
The signing of the SALT I treaty
questions.explain: The Brezhnev Doctrine was used to justify crushing the Prague Spring when Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968.

questions.q: What is meant by 'détente' in the context of the 1970s Cold War?
options: A relaxation of tension and improved relations between the superpowers
An intensification of the arms race
A total end to all diplomacy
questions.explain: Détente described the easing of superpower tension in the 1970s, reflected in agreements such as the SALT arms-limitation talks.

questions.q: In which year did the Soviet Union invade Afghanistan, an event that badly damaged détente?
questions.explain: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 ended the period of détente and worsened East-West relations.

questions.q: Which two reform policies are most associated with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev after 1985?
questions.explain: Gorbachev introduced glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) to reform the Soviet system.

questions.q: What did Gorbachev's policy of 'perestroika' involve?
options: Restructuring and reforming the Soviet economy
Building a new wall in Berlin
questions.explain: Perestroika, meaning 'restructuring', aimed to modernise and partly liberalise the stagnant Soviet economy.

questions.q: In 1989 Gorbachev made clear the USSR would not use force to prop up Eastern European communist regimes. What was a direct consequence?
options: The fall of the Berlin Wall and collapse of communist governments across Eastern Europe
The building of a second Berlin Wall
The re-formation of the Warsaw Pact
A Soviet invasion of West Germany
questions.explain: Without the threat of Soviet intervention, communist regimes fell across Eastern Europe and the Berlin Wall came down in November 1989.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE History (4HI1) specification; The Cold War 1943-91
